title: Endpoint Buying Criteria — Mapping Redwood Angle
body:
Purpose:
Quick operational playbook for AEs/SEs to map buyer selection criteria for managed endpoints and position Redwood in field conversations versus AWS/GCP/Azure managed endpoint offerings. Focus is on operator/infra and platform-engineering personas (not just product PMs). Document is intentionally tactical — scripts, one-liners, and quick rebuttals for common traps.

Status: draft — use as living cheat-sheet. Feedback loop: capture top 3 objections per account and drop into JIRA-MLSALE-482.

Target personas and decision context:
- Platform/Infra Engineer (primary): cares about predictable p99, autoscaling behavior, cost attribution, and SRE ownership boundaries.
- ML Platform/ML Engineer (primary): cares about model versioning, kv-cache portability, telemetry for quality/regression, and CI for model rollouts.
- Security/Compliance (secondary): needs VPC options, KMS/HSM, audit trails, and ability to air-gap.
- Product/ML leadership (secondary): cares about unit economics, time to production, and guardrails for model quality.

Top buying criteria (ranked by frequency across deals):
1) Latency SLOs & tail behavior (p95/p99) — customers choose a provider that gives deterministic tails under mixed workloads.
2) Cost predictability & unit economics — transparent per-token and per-inference breakdown with tooling to reduce spend.
3) Deployment control & flexibility — dedicated capacity, region/locality, private control plane.
4) Operational visibility — tracing, token-level cost, prompt-level quality dashboards.
5) Reliability & graceful degradation — fallback routing, model variant compatibility.
6) Security & compliance — VPC/air-gap, KMS, audit logs, SOC/ISO artifacts.
7) Model lifecycle & rollouts — canary, A/B, automatic fallback, and model pinning.

How Redwood maps to criteria (straight-to-field messaging):
- Latency: "Deterministic tails, engineered for production: continuous batching + KV-cache optimized kernels reduce p99 volatility compared to multi-tenant endpoints."
- Cost predictability: "Per-route token and compute attribution plus Optimize suggestions — customers lower unit cost without blind quantization."
- Deployment flexibility: "One API across hosted, Dedicated, and Private — same rollout and observability primitives wherever you run."
- Observability: "Token-level cost/latency, per-prompt regression detection, and tracing hooks developers actually use in debugging."
- Reliability: "Smart routing and model fallbacks keep apps live; Dedicated pools give predictable throughput when it matters."
- Security: "Private control plane for regulated workloads, KMS integrations, and on-prem package option."
- Rollouts: "Built-in canaries and automatic fallback policies to avoid taking production down during model swaps."

Competitive shorthand: what AWS/GCP/Azure are strong at vs typical Redwood rebuttals
- AWS/Azure/GCP strengths:
  - Deep integration with cloud infra, single-bill convenience, marketplace bundles, native IAM & logging integration.
  - Familiar procurement/contract paths for enterprises who have long cloud relationships.
  - Large managed services breadth (data stores, infra services) that can reduce integration work.
- Typical gaps we exploit:
  - Black-box tails under mixed tenant workloads — hard to guarantee p99 without dedicated pools.
  - Pricing opacity or complexity when trying to reason about per-route token economics (vendor discounts & hidden egress).
  - Limited model lifecycle tooling oriented specifically to inference (most offer training pipelines but not inference-first rollouts/quality dashboards).
  - Marketplace lock-in expectations; customers often end up tying business logic to cloud-specific features.

Direct field rebuttals / scripts (short):
- Objection: "We’re already on AWS/Azure — why switch?"
  - Script: "Totally get it. Most customers keep their infra on the cloud but adopt Redwood for inference because we reduce predictable cost and deliver stable latency under production load — while still integrating with your existing IAM and VPC. Think of us as swap-in inference runtime with better economics and SLOs."
- Objection: "Our procurement prefers single-vendor to simplify support."
  - Script: "We’re frequently deployed alongside existing cloud relationships; we provide clear SLA boundaries and can run in VPC/private deployments to meet procurement and compliance needs while improving unit economics."
- Objection: "Cloud vendor has 'managed endpoint' — isn’t that enough?"
  - Script: "Managed endpoints solve access but not inference economics or tail latency under mixed workloads. Our runtime and routing are built specifically to sustain consistent p99 while lowering per-token costs through caching and quantization-aware execution."

Practicals for demo and POC (checklist for SEs):
- Pre-demo prep: Collect expected request shapes (sequence length distribution) and peak QPS.
- POC KPI targets: 50% reduction in p99 variability, 10–30% unit cost reduction, and rollout test with automatic fallback.
- Metrics to instrument in POC: token breakdown by route, cache hit rate, queueing latency, p50/p95/p99.
- Minimal success criteria: stable p99 under synthetic mixed-workload at target QPS + demo of canary rollback in <5 minutes.

Objection handling + escalation guide (if legal/security or procurement balk):
- Security questions -> route to Solutions Eng + Security SME for architecture review (offer on-prem package design doc).
- Pricing pushes -> propose a short-term reserved Dedicated pilot with transparent metering.
- Feature parity asks (e.g., vendor-provided model ops) -> position Redwood Optimize + integrations roadmap and offer co-innovation in the POC.

Win themes (packaging by buyer type):
- AI-native startups: emphasize unit-cost, fast iteration (forkless model rollouts), and self-serve onboarding.
- Mid-market product teams: emphasize predictable performance, per-team cost attribution, and streamlined ops.
- Enterprise regulated customers: emphasize private control plane, audit-ready logs, and on-prem deployment option.

Field experiments to validate persuasion levers (run as 4-week pilots):
1) Tail-focused POC: provide a synthetic mixed-tenant workload that highlights p99 improvement vs cloud managed endpoint (quantify improvement).
2) Cost-transparency pilot: show token-level stationing for 2 weeks and run Optimize recommendations to reduce spend; measure delta.
3) Rollout safety demo: run a canary that intentionally degrades quality and show automated fallback — capture minutes-to-recovery.

Measurable claims to use in decks (must be validated in POC before use):
- "Typical p99 reduction vs unmanaged cloud endpoints: 20–60% depending on workload mix."
- "Customers reduce per-inference spend by 10–35% after applying Optimize suggestions and caching."
- "Canary rollback times <5 minutes with automatic fallback in production setups."

Open questions / research asks (drop into research backlog):
- Need benchmark matrix for p99 under specific multi-tenant shapes vs the three major clouds (standardized test harness).
- Collect 6 customer stories where vendor-managed endpoints caused production incidents attributable to tail latency.
- Build a short one-page overlay showing step-by-step migration path from cloud-managed endpoint to Redwood Dedicated.

Quick attack cards (for AE):
- Cold outreach line: "Operator-first inference runtime that makes your p99 predictable and your bill smaller — curious how you benchmark yours today?"
- Demo hook (first 15 minutes): "We’ll show a single route at target QPS and flip a canary to show automatic fallback and rollback in real-time."
- Close ask for pilot: "Let’s run a 4-week dedicated pilot with your 2 worst-performing routes and define success metrics upfront."

Notes to self / follow-ups:
- Coordinate with Research on the benchmark matrix (JIRA-RESEARCH-121).
- Update this playbook after 3 customer pilots with recorded metrics.
- Create slide pack with one-pagers tailored for Platform, ML, and Security buyers (templates for AE).

End of document.
